title: 修复 PostgreSQL 索引膨胀与缓冲缓存问题
author: SitePoint Team
content:
PostgreSQL index bloat diagnosis is one of the most neglected aspects of database maintenance, yet it directly determines whether queries hit millisecond or second-level response times. This article walks through building a reusable SQL diagnostic toolbox that combines pgstattuple, pg_buffercache, and write amplification ratio queries into a single audit script.

Table of Contents

  • Why Index Bloat Escapes Standard Monitoring
  • Setting Up a Reproducible Test Environment with Docker
  • Diagnosing B-Tree Index Bloat with pgstattuple
  • Analyzing Buffer Cache Hit Ratios with pg_buffercache
  • Measuring Write Amplification and HOT Update Efficiency
  • Rebuilding Indexes with Zero Downtime Using REINDEX CONCURRENTLY
  • Tuning Autovacuum to Prevent Bloat Recurrence
  • The Complete Diagnostic Toolbox: postgres-perf-audit.sql
  • Common Pitfalls
  • Key Takeaways

Why Index Bloat Escapes Standard Monitoring

PostgreSQL index bloat diagnosis is one of the most neglected aspects of database maintenance, yet it directly determines whether queries hit millisecond or second-level response times. The root cause is architectural: PostgreSQL's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) implementation never updates rows in place. Every UPDATE creates a new tuple version, and every DELETE marks an old tuple as dead. While autovacuum eventually reclaims dead tuples from heap pages, B-Tree indexes accumulate empty or sparsely filled leaf pages over time. Leaf page splits, dead tuple references, and low-density pages force PostgreSQL to read more index pages per scan, degrading buffer cache efficiency even when the server appears to have ample RAM.

This article walks through building a reusable SQL diagnostic toolbox, postgres-perf-audit.sql, that combines pgstattuple, pg_buffercache, and write amplification ratio queries into a single audit script. Every query has been tested against PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17. A Docker-based reproducible test environment ensures readers can generate synthetic bloat safely and validate each diagnostic query before running it against production.

Leaf page splits, dead tuple references, and low-density pages force PostgreSQL to read more index pages per scan, degrading buffer cache efficiency even when the server appears to have ample RAM.

Setting Up a Reproducible Test Environment with Docker

Prerequisites

  • Docker Desktop or Docker Engine (≥20.10 recommended)
  • psql client version 15 or later (psql --version). Install via brew install postgresql (macOS) or apt install postgresql-client-17 (Debian/Ubuntu). The client major version should match the server to avoid unexpected behavior with \dx, \gexec, and other meta-commands.
  • Free TCP port 5432 on localhost (stop any existing PostgreSQL instance on that port)
  • Sufficient disk space: ~2 GB for Docker image + data volume + index rebuild scratch space

Launching PostgreSQL 17 in Docker

The fastest path to a disposable PostgreSQL instance with the right extensions is a single docker run command. The named volume ensures data persists across container restarts.

# For production, use Docker secrets or --env-file instead of -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD
docker run -d \
  --name pg17-bloat-lab \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=labpass \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -v pg17data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:17.4

# Pin to a specific minor version (e.g., postgres:17.4) to ensure reproducible results.
# Check hub.docker.com/r/library/postgres for the current latest tag.

# Connect via psql
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d postgres

Note on volume reuse: If the pg17data volume exists from a prior run, the container starts with existing data, producing inconsistent bloat results. Run docker volume rm pg17data before repeating the setup from scratch.

Installing Required Extensions

The official PostgreSQL Docker image ships both pgstattuple and pg_buffercache as contrib modules but does not enable them by default. They require superuser privileges to install because they expose low-level internal page structures and shared memory state that could leak information about other sessions' data. Querying pg_buffercache and pgstattuple requires superuser or membership in the pg_monitor role (PostgreSQL 10+).

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_buffercache;

-- Verify installation
\dx pgstattuple
\dx pg_buffercache

-- Alternative verification:
SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension
WHERE extname IN ('pgstattuple', 'pg_buffercache');

The \dx output should show both extensions with their schema set to public (whichever schema was first in search_path at install time) and the version matching the PostgreSQL major release.

Generating Synthetic Bloat

Generate controlled bloat to validate diagnostic queries before trusting their output in production. The following script creates a table with a B-Tree index, inserts 500,000 rows, then updates 80% of them. Because the UPDATE modifies an indexed column (status), PostgreSQL cannot use HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates, forcing new index entries for every modified row and leaving dead references in the B-Tree.

Non-determinism note: The INSERT uses random(), so exact bloat metrics will differ across runs. The expected output values shown later in this article are illustrative, not exact.

-- Create table and index
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    amount NUMERIC(10,2),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status);

-- Bulk insert 500K rows
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, amount)
SELECT
    (random() * 10000)::int,
    'pending',
    (random() * 1000)::numeric(10,2)
FROM generate_series(1, 500000);

-- Mass update 80% to generate bloat in the index
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'processed'
WHERE id <= 400000;

-- Run VACUUM to clean heap dead tuples but leave index bloat intact
VACUUM orders;
ANALYZE orders;

After this sequence, the heap is relatively clean but idx_orders_status retains the dead index entries and fragmented leaf pages that are the target of the diagnostic queries below.

Autovacuum interference: Autovacuum may run between the UPDATE and the diagnostic queries, reducing observed bloat. If you need exact bloat levels for testing, disable autovacuum on the test table: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);

Diagnosing B-Tree Index Bloat with pgstattuple

Understanding B-Tree Internal Fragmentation

B-Tree indexes in PostgreSQL organize data across internal (branch) pages and leaf pages. When a leaf page fills up, it splits into two pages, each roughly half full. DELETE and UPDATE operations scatter dead tuple pointers across leaf pages over time, but unlike heap pages, indexes do not benefit from HOT updates. HOT updates bypass index insertion only when no indexed column changes, the new tuple fits on the same heap page, and the heap page has sufficient free space, as reserved by fillfactor. When an indexed column does change, every index on the table receives a new entry.

The key metric is avg_leaf_density: the average percentage of usable space on leaf pages. Target leaf density above 70%; below that threshold, the index is physically larger than it needs to be, each index scan touches more pages, and those oversized pages compete for space in shared_buffers. (The 70% threshold appears frequently in the PostgreSQL wiki and community tooling. It is a practical heuristic, not a hard database limit.)

Table bloat and index bloat are distinct problems. A table can have minimal dead tuples (thanks to autovacuum) while its indexes remain severely bloated. This asymmetry is what makes index bloat easy to miss during routine monitoring.

Running the Bloat Estimation Query

The pgstatindex function (part of the pgstattuple extension) returns a single-row result describing the physical structure of a B-Tree index. The critical columns are avg_leaf_density (average fill percentage of leaf pages), leaf_fragmentation (percentage of leaf pages out of logical order), empty_pages (leaf pages with zero live tuples), and deleted_pages (pages marked for recycling).

-- Analyze the bloated index
SELECT
    version,                    -- B-Tree version (typically 4)
    tree_level,                 -- Depth of the B-Tree
    index_size,                 -- Total index size in bytes
    leaf_pages,                 -- Number of leaf pages
    empty_pages,                -- Leaf pages with zero tuples
    deleted_pages,              -- Pages marked for recycling
    avg_leaf_density,           -- Target: > 70%. Below = bloat
    leaf_fragmentation          -- 0-100: logical vs physical order
FROM pgstatindex('idx_orders_status');

/*  Expected output after mass update + VACUUM (approximate; values will vary):
 version | tree_level | index_size | leaf_pages | empty_pages | deleted_pages | avg_leaf_density | leaf_fragmentation
---------+------------+------------+------------+-------------+---------------+------------------+--------------------
       4 |          2 |   20480000 |       2490 |         412 |           187 |            52.30 |              38.70
*/

Thresholds for action: an avg_leaf_density below 70% warrants investigation; below 50% is a strong signal to reindex. These are operational heuristics, not hard PostgreSQL limits. A leaf_fragmentation above 30% combined with low density indicates the index is both oversized and poorly ordered on disk, compounding sequential read penalties.

Scanning All Indexes for Bloat at Scale

Checking indexes one at a time does not scale. The following query joins pg_catalog.pg_indexes with pgstatindex() to produce a ranked bloat report across all schemas. This is the first major component of the postgres-perf-audit.sql toolbox.

-- All-index bloat report (Component 1 of postgres-perf-audit.sql)
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '60s';

SELECT
    schemaname AS schema,
    tablename AS table,
    indexname AS index,
    pg_size_pretty(s.index_size::bigint) AS index_size,
    s.avg_leaf_density,
    s.leaf_fragmentation,
    s.empty_pages,
    s.deleted_pages
FROM pg_indexes
JOIN pg_class ic
  ON ic.relname      = indexname
 AND ic.relkind      = 'i'
 AND ic.relam        = (SELECT oid FROM pg_am WHERE amname = 'btree')
 AND ic.relnamespace = (SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = schemaname),
     LATERAL pgstatindex((schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass) AS s
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
ORDER BY s.avg_leaf_density ASC
LIMIT 30;

A critical performance caveat: pgstatindex reads every page of the target index sequentially. A 1 GB index means 1 GB of sequential reads. Additionally, pgstatindex acquires a ShareLock on each index, which blocks concurrent DDL operations on that relation. On a database with hundreds of large indexes, this query can take minutes and saturate disk I/O. Schedule it during low-traffic maintenance windows, not during peak hours.

Analyzing Buffer Cache Hit Ratios with pg_buffercache

What the Buffer Cache Hit Ratio Actually Tells You

The standard PostgreSQL buffer cache hit ratio formula is blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read) from pg_stat_database. Many teams target a 99% ratio, but this number is misleading in the presence of index bloat. Bloated indexes inflate blks_hit because PostgreSQL dutifully caches bloated pages in shared_buffers. Those pages contain mostly dead space, yet they count as "hits," displacing genuinely useful heap and index data. A 99.5% hit ratio on a database with severe index bloat can mask the fact that a meaningful fraction of cached pages are waste.

A 99.5% hit ratio on a database with severe index bloat can mask the fact that a meaningful fraction of cached pages are waste.

-- Database-level cache hit ratio (Component 2 of postgres-perf-audit.sql)
SELECT
    datname,
    blks_hit,
    blks_read,
    CASE WHEN (blks_hit + blks_read) > 0
         THEN round(100.0 * blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read), 2)
         ELSE 0
    END AS cache_hit_ratio_pct,
    stats_reset
FROM pg_stat_database
WHERE datname = current_database();

Note: blks_hit and blks_read accumulate since the last pg_stat_reset() call or server restart. Check pg_stat_database.stats_reset to understand the measurement window before interpreting this ratio.

A high ratio here is necessary but not sufficient. The per-relation breakdown reveals whether that ratio is backed by useful data or bloated pages.

Per-Relation Buffer Cache Breakdown

The pg_buffercache view exposes every page currently in shared_buffers, linked to its source relation. Joining it with pg_class via pg_filenode_relation() safely resolves each buffer page to its owning relation, even after operations like REINDEX, VACUUM FULL, or TRUNCATE that reassign a relation's file node.

-- Per-relation buffer cache breakdown (Component 3 of postgres-perf-audit.sql)
SELECT
    c.relname                                           AS relation,
    CASE c.relkind
        WHEN 'r' THEN 'table'
        WHEN 'i' THEN 'index'
        WHEN 't' THEN 'toast'
        WHEN 'm' THEN 'matview'
        ELSE c.relkind
    END                                                 AS type,
    count(*)                                            AS buffer_pages,
    pg_size_pretty(
        count(*) * current_setting('block_size')::bigint
    )                                                   AS buffered_size,
    round(
        100.0 * count(*) / NULLIF(
            (SELECT count(*)
               FROM pg_buffercache
              WHERE relblocknumber IS NOT NULL),
            0
        ),
        2
    )                                                   AS pct_of_cache
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c
  ON c.oid = pg_filenode_relation(b.reltablespace, b.relfilenode)
WHERE b.relblocknumber IS NOT NULL
  AND b.relfilenode IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.relname, c.relkind
ORDER BY buffer_pages DESC
LIMIT 20;

Correlating Bloat with Cache Inefficiency

After running the synthetic bloat scenario, the bloated idx_orders_status typically occupies a disproportionate share of the buffer cache relative to its useful data density. If pgstatindex reports 48% average leaf density and the buffer cache breakdown shows the index consuming 15% of shared_buffers, then 7.8% of total buffer memory (48% of that 15%) holds dead space. That is RAM that could otherwise cache hot heap pages or frequently accessed non-bloated indexes. On a server with 8 GB of shared_buffers, 7.8% translates to over 600 MB of wasted cache capacity.

Measuring Write Amplification and HOT Update Efficiency

What Is Write Amplification in PostgreSQL?

Write amplification in PostgreSQL refers to the ratio of physical writes (across the heap and all indexes) to the logical writes a user actually issues. A single UPDATE on a table with five indexes can generate six physical writes: one for the new heap tuple and one new entry in each index. HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates short-circuit this process. When a row update does not modify any indexed column and the new tuple version fits on the same heap page, PostgreSQL skips all index insertions. This is the single most effective mechanism for reducing index bloat organically.

HOT updates fail when:

  • An indexed column is modified
  • The target heap page lacks free space (controlled by fillfactor)
  • The updated tuple is too large to fit on the same page
  • The fillfactor is set to 100 (the default for heap tables), leaving no room for in-page tuple storage

Querying the Write Amplification Ratio

The pg_stat_user_tables view exposes the columns needed to calculate both write amplification and HOT update efficiency per table. The write_amplification_ratio metric below represents the effective average number of physical writes per logical update: 1 (for the heap) plus the fraction of non-HOT updates multiplied by the index count. When HOT% is 0, every update touches all indexes, so the ratio equals 1 + index_count. When HOT% is 100, no index writes occur, and the ratio equals 1.

-- Write amplification & HOT ratio report (Component 4 of postgres-perf-audit.sql)
-- write_amplification_ratio = effective average physical writes per update
-- = 1 (heap) + non_HOT_fraction * index_count
WITH index_counts AS (
    SELECT indrelid, count(*) AS index_count
      FROM pg_index
     GROUP BY indrelid
)
SELECT
    s.schemaname,
    s.relname AS table_name,
    s.n_tup_upd AS total_updates,
    s.n_tup_hot_upd AS hot_updates,
    CASE WHEN s.n_tup_upd > 0
         THEN round(100.0 * s.n_tup_hot_upd / s.n_tup_upd, 2)
         ELSE 0
    END AS hot_update_pct,
    s.n_dead_tup AS dead_tuples,
    s.n_tup_mod_since_analyze AS mods_since_analyze,
    COALESCE(ic.index_count, 0) AS index_count,
    CASE WHEN s.n_tup_upd > 0
         THEN round(
                  1.0 + (
                      (s.n_tup_upd - s.n_tup_hot_upd)::numeric
                      / s.n_tup_upd
                  ) * COALESCE(ic.index_count, 0),
                  2
              )
         ELSE 1
    END AS write_amplification_ratio
FROM pg_stat_user_tables s
LEFT JOIN index_counts ic ON ic.indrelid = s.relid
WHERE s.n_tup_upd > 100  -- minimum update threshold; adjust for low-traffic tables
ORDER BY hot_update_pct ASC;

A HOT update percentage below 50% on a high-write table is an actionable signal worth investigating. It means more than half of all updates are generating redundant index entries, accelerating bloat accumulation.

Tuning fillfactor to Encourage HOT Updates

Setting fillfactor below 100 reserves a percentage of each heap page for future in-page tuple updates, directly enabling HOT when indexed columns are not modified. A fillfactor of 85 reserves 15% of each page, which works well for tables receiving under 10K updates per hour on non-indexed columns.

-- Reserve 15% of each page for HOT updates
ALTER TABLE orders SET (fillfactor = 85);

-- Note: PostgreSQL applies this setting only to pages it writes after the ALTER.
-- To apply retroactively, run VACUUM FULL or use pg_repack.

The trade-off is disk space. A fillfactor of 85 means the heap is approximately 17.6% larger than it would be at 100 (1 / 0.85 = 1.176). For tables where updates rarely touch indexed columns, this trade-off pays for itself many times over through reduced index write amplification and slower bloat accumulation.

Rebuilding Indexes with Zero Downtime Using REINDEX CONCURRENTLY

Why REINDEX CONCURRENTLY Over Regular REINDEX

A standard REINDEX takes an AccessExclusiveLock on the index, which blocks all reads and writes to the underlying table for the duration of the rebuild. On a large index, this can mean minutes of downtime. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, introduced in PostgreSQL 12, builds a replacement index without holding a table lock. It cannot be used on indexes supporting exclusion constraints, cannot run inside a transaction block, and cannot target system catalog indexes. Expect 1.5-2x the wall-clock time of a standard REINDEX, depending on concurrent write load, because the process must track concurrent changes. It also requires temporary disk space roughly equal to the current index size plus WAL overhead.

Disk space warning: Each concurrent reindex temporarily doubles the disk space used by that index. Verify available disk space with df -h on the data directory and check pg_database_size() before proceeding.

Automating REINDEX for Bloated Indexes

The following script queries the bloat report, filters indexes exceeding a configurable density threshold, and generates executable REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY statements. This is the fifth component of the diagnostic toolbox. Review the generated statements before executing them by pasting into an interactive psql session.

-- Automated REINDEX CONCURRENTLY generator (Component 5 of postgres-perf-audit.sql)
-- Adjust the threshold (avg_leaf_density < 65) as needed

-- DRY RUN: This query only generates statements. Copy the output and
-- paste into an interactive psql session. Append \gexec to execute.
-- Each concurrent reindex temporarily doubles disk space used by that index.
-- Verify available disk space before proceeding.

SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '60s';

SELECT format(
    'REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY %I.%I;',
    schemaname, indexname
)
FROM pg_indexes
JOIN pg_class ic
  ON ic.relname      = indexname
 AND ic.relkind      = 'i'
 AND ic.relam        = (SELECT oid FROM pg_am WHERE amname = 'btree')
 AND ic.relnamespace = (SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = schemaname),
     LATERAL pgstatindex((schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass) AS s
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND s.avg_leaf_density < 65
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
        FROM pg_class orphan
        JOIN pg_namespace ns ON ns.oid = orphan.relnamespace
       WHERE orphan.relname LIKE indexname || '_ccnew%'
         AND ns.nspname = schemaname
  )
ORDER BY s.avg_leaf_density ASC;

The NOT EXISTS check against the _ccnew% pattern prevents the script from attempting to reindex an index that is already mid-rebuild from a concurrent operation (PostgreSQL may append _ccnew or _ccnew_NNN with a numeric suffix). The namespace filter ensures the check only considers temporary indexes in the same schema. Copy the generated statements and paste them into an interactive psql session, appending \gexec to execute. Note that \gexec is a psql-specific meta-command; it does not work in GUI tools (pgAdmin, DBeaver) or when running via psql -c.

Verifying the Results

After the concurrent reindex completes, re-run the diagnostic queries to confirm the improvement. The query below uses a single LATERAL call to pgstatindex to avoid scanning the index twice.

-- Before/after comparison (single pgstatindex call via LATERAL)
SELECT
    'AFTER REINDEX'                                              AS phase,
    indexname,
    pg_size_pretty(s.index_size::bigint)                         AS index_size,
    s.avg_leaf_density,
    s.leaf_fragmentation,
    (SELECT count(*)
       FROM pg_buffercache
      WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(
                (schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass
            )
    )                                                            AS buffer_pages
FROM pg_indexes,
     LATERAL pgstatindex(
         (schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass
     ) AS s
WHERE indexname = 'idx_orders_status';

/* After reindex, avg_leaf_density should jump above 90% and
   buffer_pages should drop proportionally as the index shrinks. */

Tuning Autovacuum to Prevent Bloat Recurrence

Key Autovacuum Parameters for High-Write Tables

Default autovacuum settings are conservative. For tables with disproportionate update rates, per-table overrides ensure vacuum keeps pace with dead tuple generation.

ALTER TABLE orders SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,   -- Trigger at 2% dead tuples (default: 20%)
    autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2,         -- Reduce sleep between vacuum I/O rounds (default: 2ms since PG13; was 20ms in PG12 and earlier)
    autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 1000       -- Allow more work per round (default: 200)
);
-- autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02 means vacuum triggers after ~10K dead tuples on a 500K row table
-- instead of waiting for 100K dead tuples at the default 0.20 threshold.

Monitoring Autovacuum Effectiveness

Regularly check that autovacuum is actually keeping pace with write volume.

SELECT
    relname,
    last_autovacuum,
    last_autoanalyze,
    n_dead_tup,
    autovacuum_count,
    n_tup_upd,
    CASE WHEN n_tup_upd > 0
         THEN round(100.0 * n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_upd, 2)
         ELSE 0
    END AS hot_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'orders';

If n_dead_tup climbs steadily between last_autovacuum timestamps, the cost limit or scale factor needs further tuning.

The Complete Diagnostic Toolbox: postgres-perf-audit.sql

The five query components from the preceding sections consolidate into a single, copy-paste-ready SQL file. Run it as a weekly cron job during a low-traffic maintenance window and pipe output to a Slack webhook or monitoring dashboard for ongoing visibility.

Bloat is a recurring condition driven by MVCC mechanics, not a one-time fix. Running the diagnostic toolbox on a regular schedule turns index maintenance from ad-hoc incident response into a scheduled operation.

-- =============================================================
-- postgres-perf-audit.sql
-- PostgreSQL Performance Audit Toolbox (PG 15/16/17)
-- Usage: psql -h HOST -U USER -d DBNAME -f postgres-perf-audit.sql
-- Requires: pgstattuple, pg_buffercache extensions
-- Schedule: weekly via cron during low-traffic window
--
-- NOTE: pgstatindex acquires a ShareLock on each index during its
-- scan. On busy systems, schedule accordingly.
-- =============================================================

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
SET statement_timeout = '60s';  -- adjust to index size; reset after if needed

-- Extensions pre-check
DO $$
BEGIN
    IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pgstattuple') THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'pgstattuple extension not installed. Run: CREATE EXTENSION pgstattuple;';
    END IF;
    IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_buffercache') THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'pg_buffercache extension not installed. Run: CREATE EXTENSION pg_buffercache;';
    END IF;
END;
$$;

-- 1. All-Index Bloat Report
\echo '=== INDEX BLOAT REPORT ==='
SELECT schemaname AS schema, tablename AS table, indexname AS index,
       pg_size_pretty(s.index_size::bigint) AS index_size,
       s.avg_leaf_density,
       s.leaf_fragmentation,
       s.empty_pages,
       s.deleted_pages
FROM pg_indexes
JOIN pg_class ic
  ON ic.relname      = indexname
 AND ic.relkind      = 'i'
 AND ic.relam        = (SELECT oid FROM pg_am WHERE amname = 'btree')
 AND ic.relnamespace = (SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = schemaname),
     LATERAL pgstatindex((schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass) AS s
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
ORDER BY s.avg_leaf_density ASC LIMIT 30;

-- 2. Database-Level Cache Hit Ratio
\echo '=== CACHE HIT RATIO ==='
\echo '(Counters are cumulative since last pg_stat_reset() — check stats_reset column for window)'
SELECT datname, blks_hit, blks_read,
       CASE WHEN (blks_hit+blks_read)>0 THEN round(100.0*blks_hit/(blks_hit+blks_read),2) ELSE 0 END AS cache_hit_ratio_pct,
       stats_reset
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

-- 3. Per-Relation Buffer Cache Breakdown
\echo '=== BUFFER CACHE BY RELATION ==='
SELECT
    c.relname                                           AS relation,
    CASE c.relkind
        WHEN 'r' THEN 'table'
        WHEN 'i' THEN 'index'
        WHEN 't' THEN 'toast'
        WHEN 'm' THEN 'matview'
        ELSE c.relkind
    END                                                 AS type,
    count(*)                                            AS buffer_pages,
    pg_size_pretty(
        count(*) * current_setting('block_size')::bigint
    )                                                   AS buffered_size,
    round(
        100.0 * count(*) / NULLIF(
            (SELECT count(*)
               FROM pg_buffercache
              WHERE relblocknumber IS NOT NULL),
            0
        ),
        2
    )                                                   AS pct_of_cache
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c
  ON c.oid = pg_filenode_relation(b.reltablespace, b.relfilenode)
WHERE b.relblocknumber IS NOT NULL
  AND b.relfilenode IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.relname, c.relkind
ORDER BY buffer_pages DESC LIMIT 20;

-- 4. Write Amplification & HOT Ratio
\echo '=== WRITE AMPLIFICATION ==='
WITH index_counts AS (
    SELECT indrelid, count(*) AS index_count
      FROM pg_index
     GROUP BY indrelid
)
SELECT
    s.schemaname,
    s.relname AS table_name,
    s.n_tup_upd AS total_updates,
    s.n_tup_hot_upd AS hot_updates,
    CASE WHEN s.n_tup_upd > 0
         THEN round(100.0 * s.n_tup_hot_upd / s.n_tup_upd, 2)
         ELSE 0
    END AS hot_update_pct,
    s.n_dead_tup AS dead_tuples,
    COALESCE(ic.index_count, 0) AS index_count,
    CASE WHEN s.n_tup_upd > 0
         THEN round(
                  1.0 + (
                      (s.n_tup_upd - s.n_tup_hot_upd)::numeric
                      / s.n_tup_upd
                  ) * COALESCE(ic.index_count, 0),
                  2
              )
         ELSE 1
    END AS write_amplification_ratio
FROM pg_stat_user_tables s
LEFT JOIN index_counts ic ON ic.indrelid = s.relid
WHERE s.n_tup_upd > 100  -- minimum update threshold; adjust for low-traffic tables
ORDER BY hot_update_pct ASC;

-- 5. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY Generator
-- IMPORTANT: Component 5 generates REINDEX statements but does NOT execute them.
-- Review the output, then paste into an interactive psql session and append \gexec to execute.
-- Do NOT add \gexec to this file for automated/cron execution without manual review.
\echo '=== REINDEX CANDIDATES (paste into psql with \\gexec to execute) ==='
SELECT format('REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY %I.%I;', schemaname, indexname)
FROM pg_indexes
JOIN pg_class ic
  ON ic.relname      = indexname
 AND ic.relkind      = 'i'
 AND ic.relam        = (SELECT oid FROM pg_am WHERE amname = 'btree')
 AND ic.relnamespace = (SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = schemaname),
     LATERAL pgstatindex((schemaname || '.' || indexname)::regclass) AS s
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
  AND s.avg_leaf_density < 65
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
        FROM pg_class orphan
        JOIN pg_namespace ns ON ns.oid = orphan.relnamespace
       WHERE orphan.relname LIKE indexname || '_ccnew%'
         AND ns.nspname = schemaname
  )
ORDER BY s.avg_leaf_density ASC;

Common Pitfalls

  • \gexec only works in psql: It does not function in GUI tools (pgAdmin, DBeaver) or when invoked via psql -c. Use interactive psql or psql -f mode.
  • Port conflicts: If another PostgreSQL instance occupies port 5432, use -p 5433:5432 in the docker run command and connect with psql -p 5433.
  • Volume reuse: The named Docker volume pg17data persists data across container restarts. Clear it with docker volume rm pg17data before re-running the full setup to get consistent bloat baselines.
  • Each pgstatindex call reads every page of its target index sequentially and acquires a ShareLock. On hundreds of large indexes, a 10 GB index means 10 GB of sequential reads per call, and concurrent DDL on each scanned index will block until the scan finishes. Always run during maintenance windows.
  • Non-B-Tree indexes: pgstatindex only supports B-Tree indexes. Running it against GIN, GiST, BRIN, or hash indexes raises an error. The queries in this toolbox filter for B-Tree indexes via pg_am to avoid this.

Key Takeaways

Index bloat degrades query performance and wastes buffer cache. Measuring it through pgstatindex is non-negotiable for any table where n_tup_upd exceeds a few thousand rows per hour. An avg_leaf_density below 70% or a HOT update ratio below 50% should trigger investigation. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY eliminates bloat without downtime but must be paired with per-table autovacuum tuning and fillfactor adjustments to prevent recurrence. Bloat is a recurring condition driven by MVCC mechanics, not a one-time fix. Running the diagnostic toolbox on a regular schedule turns index maintenance from ad-hoc incident response into a scheduled operation.

oneSentenceSummary: 本技术指南提供了一套全面的 SQL 诊断工具箱，利用 pgstattuple 和 pg_buffercache 来识别并解决 PostgreSQL 的索引膨胀、缓冲缓存低效以及写放大问题。
summary: 本文探讨了由 MVCC 架构引起的、经常被忽视的 PostgreSQL 索引膨胀问题，即更新和删除操作会在 B-Tree 索引中留下死元组引用。作者通过构建一个可复用的 SQL 工具箱，提供了一套实操的诊断方法。文中演示了如何搭建可复现的 Docker 环境来产生模拟膨胀，并使用 `pgstattuple` 扩展来衡量叶子节点密度和碎片化程度。此外，文章解释了膨胀的索引如何通过浪费共享内存来降低缓冲缓存命中率，并引入了一种计算写放大率的方法来评估 HOT（Heap-Only Tuple）更新的效率。指南最后给出了可操作的调优建议，例如使用 `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` 和调整 `fillfactor` 以减少未来的膨胀。

mainPoints.point: 索引膨胀源于 PostgreSQL 的 MVCC 架构，并通过增加 I/O 和浪费缓存来降低性能。
mainPoints.explanation: 由于 PostgreSQL 从不就地更新行，B-Tree 索引会积累空闲或填充稀疏的叶子页。这迫使数据库在每次扫描时读取更多页面，即使系统 RAM 充足，也会将缓冲缓存中的有用数据挤出。

mainPoints.point: `pgstattuple` 扩展可以精确测量 B-Tree 的内部碎片化。
mainPoints.explanation: 通过使用 `pgstatindex`，开发者可以监控 `avg_leaf_density`。密度低于 70% 通常表示存在膨胀，低于 50% 则是重新索引的强烈信号，因为这表明索引的物理尺寸超过了实际需要。

mainPoints.point: 在存在索引膨胀的情况下，标准的缓冲缓存命中率可能会产生误导。
mainPoints.explanation: 高命中率（例如 99.5%）可能会掩盖低效问题，因为 PostgreSQL 也会缓存膨胀的页面。这些页面包含大量死空间，但仍被计为「命中」，实际上浪费了 `shared_buffers` 内存的一部分。

mainPoints.point: 写放大和 HOT 更新效率对于防止膨胀再次出现至关重要。
mainPoints.explanation: 当索引列未被修改且堆页有足够空间时，HOT 更新可以绕过索引插入。较低的 HOT 更新百分比意味着较高的写放大，即每次逻辑更新都会在所有索引中产生多次物理写入。

mainPoints.point: 调优 `fillfactor` 是实现更多 HOT 更新的主要策略。
mainPoints.explanation: 将 `fillfactor` 从默认的 100 降低到较低数值（例如 85），可以为每个堆页预留未来更新的空间，从而允许数据库执行 HOT 更新并降低索引膨胀率。

keyQuotes: 叶子页分裂、死元组引用和低密度页面迫使 PostgreSQL 在每次扫描时读取更多索引页，即使服务器看起来有充足的 RAM，也会降低缓冲缓存的效率。
在索引严重膨胀的数据库中，99.5% 的命中率可能会掩盖这样一个事实：缓存页面中有相当一部分是浪费的。
只有在没有索引列发生变化、新元组能放入同一个堆页且堆页有足够空闲空间（由 fillfactor 预留）的情况下，HOT 更新才能绕过索引插入。
